newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -U.S. Jan CPI seen showing tame inflation.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -U.S. Jan CPI seen showing tame inflation.

text.p: The U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) is expected to rise 0.3 percent in January, yet another indication that inflation remains tame, economists said.

Should the figure come in as expected, it would provide more welcome news to bond market participants following the 0.3 percent decrease seen in January producer prices last week -- the first decline since October of 1994.
Economists polled by Reuters also expected the "core" rate, excluding the volatile food and energy components, would rise 0.2 percent in the month.
The U.S. Labor Department will release the number at 0830 EST/1330 GMT Wednesday.

"CPI will be the most important number this week, particularly in light of the strong rally seen on PPI. But quite often, these two numbers don't match too well on a month-to-month basis, " said William Dudley, senior economist at Goldman Sachs & Co.
Dudley expected to see rises of 0.3 percent in both the overall and core rates. He said signs of inflationary pressures in the services sector may begin to exert themselves in the report.

Charles Lieberman, director of financial markets research at Chase Securities Inc., also expected both figures to rise 0.3 percent. He said increasing hotel costs would begin to show up in the core rate and added that the food and energy components were holding up.
"On balance, it will be a touch higher, but nothing shocking," Lieberman said. "Inflation remains contained."

"The market may be set up for a little disappointment as no bad numbers have been factored in," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. He saw total CPI rising 0.3 percent and the core rate up 0.2 percent.
Moran said some companies have a tendency to raise prices at the beginning of the year, which may contribute to the rise in the core rate.

"New and used car prices were contained and there were a lot of sales on apparel to clear shelves, but energy could remain a problem," Moran said. "Import prices were well behaved due to the strength of the dollar."
Economists at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc said mild inflation combined with weakening food and energy price pressures would make for a tame CPI figure in January.

They forecast core inflation stable at about 2.5 percent annually, although they said seasonal influences and anecdotal reports of less discounting relative to recent years added limited upside risks.
They noted that energy prices have begun to ease after several large monthly increases.
